To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the cerebral cortex can be divided into two main subsystem, one for external stimuli processing and one for processing of body and self; and 2) the latter system is modulated by the manipulation of the degree of ‘projection’ of the body border.

(i) the brain is organized as a bipartite network, with one part processing extrinsic and one part processing intrinsic information; (ii) the intrinsic part is related to the body and the self, and (iii) this part is modulated by the degree of ‘body-self projection’.

the ‘intrinsic’ and ‘extrinsic’ system of the human cortex can be differentiated on the basis of the manipulation of self-location and that these systems are functionally and anatomically segregated in the human cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental issue: the nature of the human cortex.
the neural mechanisms that underlie the processing of external stimuli and internal information.
the question of how the human brain processes information about the body and self, and how these processes are linked to the processing of information from external sources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-projection is an intrinsic component that is added to the extrinsic information received by the cortex.
there are at least two systems in the human cortex: an ‘extrinsic’ one and an ‘intrinsic’ one.
there are two main subsystems in the human cortex, an ‘extrinsic’ one and an ‘intrinsic’ one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
self-projection is an important component of human cognition that is implemented in the human brain as a ‘self-projection network’.
the human cortex is organized into a dual system: an ‘extrinsic’ system for external stimuli processing and an ‘intrinsic’ one for processing the internal milieu of body and self.
the ‘extrinsic’ system is related to processing of external stimuli and the ‘intrinsic’ one is related to processing and integration of information about the internal milieu of the body and self.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self-projection is a process involving a distributed cortical network that is not necessarily confined to the mirror neuron system.
the ‘intrinsic’ subsystem is not only involved in processing of the ‘body schema’, but is also engaged in the representation of the ‘self’.
the human cortex has an ‘intrinsic’ and an ‘extrinsic’ subsystem, which can be identified by the degree of self-projection of the stimulus.
